items.title: [bitterteaandmystery.blogspot.com] Station Eternity: Mur Lafferty
items.content_html:
This book has been on my TBR stack for a while; I borrowed it from my son soon after he bought at the Planned Parenthood book sale two years ago. I wanted to read this book because I was looking for science fiction books set on a space station. This fits the bill for sure, but it is also a first contact story and a mystery. There are even some elements of spy fiction, since the US military sends a spy to the station with several missions. 


At the beginning of the book, the setting is the space station, Station Eternity. The station is sentient, and has control over who can board the space station. Most of the beings on board the space station are aliens. There are many different alien species on the station; one of them is the Gneiss, who are very large and look like rocks. Another species is very small. They resemble the wasps on earth and are called the Sundry. Some of the Sundry are blue, some are silver, and they have their differences. 

Initially, only three humans have been allowed on the station: The ambassador from earth, who achieved his position due to his facility with languages, and doesn't have a clue about diplomacy; Mallory Veridian; and Xan Morgan ("Xan" is short for Alexander). Mallory and Xan are both in their early thirties, I am guessing, and they knew each other on earth before they were given sanctuary by Station Eternity. 

The book is divided into three sections. The first section introduces Mallory, Xan, and some of the aliens, plus details Mallory's experiences on the space station. At the end of Part One, a shuttle with visitors from earth has arrived and there has been a mishap when the shuttle attempts to dock with the Station Eternity. 

In Part Two, the point of view shifts away from Mallory to various aliens and the new arrivals from earth, and provides more background information for Xan. Several of the humans who were chosen to visit are connected to either Mallory or Xan in some way. Much of the story is revealed in flashbacks in this section, and that can be confusing. 

The third section pulls together several ongoing plots with both the aliens and the humans, and resolves the mystery plot.


My Thoughts:

  • I am glad I finally read Station Eternity; it was the perfect story for me and especially at this time. I needed a book with humor. It was longer, at 445 pages, but it was also fast-paced, which made it an easier read. The first contact story was unusual (at least it seemed so to me since I haven't read that much science fiction), and a good mystery too. 
  • The book I read prior to this book was The Good Thief's Guide to Amsterdam by Chris Ewan. The main character in that book was a thief who also writes mysteries about a thief. I was surprised to find that the main character in this book, Mallory, also writes mysteries. In this case she writes mysteries because no one will hire her for any job because everywhere she goes, murders occur. So she writes thinly veiled mystery fiction about her life.
  • This is also a story about families and relationships. When the humans on the shuttle arrive, a lot of them have connections to either Xan or Mallory (or both). And there is a grandmother who has brought her granddaughter to the station because she thinks that the aliens can cure her granddaughter's injuries. 
  • There are some challenges in reading this book. There are a lot characters. Combine that with the changes in point of view characters and the frequent use of short flashbacks, and it can get confusing. Some of the scenes with the aliens were over my head. But none of that bothered me. I loved it from beginning to end.
  • This is the first book in the Midsolar Murders Series, and I will be getting book 2 in the series.
